summary: Describes the IS-IS extensions needed to run Segment Routing over the IPv6 data plane. Segment Routing encodes a path as a list of segments, and this document lets IS-IS advertise the information routers need for that on IPv6. It updates RFC 7370 by modifying a registry.

plainLanguage.summary: Segment Routing lets a sender steer a packet along a list of instructions rather than letting each router pick the next hop. This RFC adds the IS-IS advertisements that let routers advertise the segment identifiers they hold and the behaviour bound to each one.

questions: what is the srv6 locator tlv
what is an srv6 end sid
subtitle: The IS-IS advertisements that let routers tell each other which SRv6 segments they have and what those segments do.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing over IPv6 needs a way for routers to advertise the segments they have and the behaviour bound to each one, but IS-IS had no extensions for it.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds a top-level SRv6 Locator TLV that announces summary prefixes for the segments at a node, plus sub-TLVs for End SIDs, adjacency SIDs, the SID structure, the router capability and the maximum SID depths.
tldr.outcome: IS-IS can now carry the information needed to run SRv6, and the document updates RFC 7370 by modifying an existing registry.

facts.label: SRv6 LAN End.X SID sub-TLV type

today: RFC 9352 is a Proposed Standard from February 2023. It updates RFC 7370 by adding the SRv6 Locator TLV to the registry of sub-TLVs for TLVs advertising prefix reachability, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Extensions Add
sections.content:
With Segment Routing, as described in RFC 8402, a node steers a packet through an ordered list of instructions called segments, and each segment is identified by a Segment Identifier (SID). Segment Routing can run over MPLS or over IPv6. The IPv6 form uses the Segment Routing Header (SRH) defined in RFC 8754, and is called SRv6.

The document builds on the network programming paradigm in RFC 8986, which describes how a behaviour can be bound to a SID and how a network program can be written as a combination of SIDs. This RFC specifies the IS-IS extensions that let IS-IS encode some of those SIDs and their behaviours, and it says that familiarity with the network programming paradigm is needed to understand the extensions.

The pieces it defines are: a new SRv6 Locator top-level TLV that announces a summary address for the set of topology- and algorithm-specific SIDs at a node; an SRv6 Capabilities sub-TLV that announces the ability to support SRv6; several new sub-TLVs that advertise the maximum SRv6 SID depths; and the SRv6 End SID, SRv6 End.X SID and SRv6 LAN End.X SID sub-TLVs, which advertise which SIDs are instantiated at a node and what Endpoint behaviour is bound to each one. The document also updates RFC 7370 by modifying an existing registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Segment Routing replaces per-hop route calculation with a list of instructions that the packet carries. This RFC adds the IS-IS advertisements that let routers advertise which of those instructions they have and what each one does.

sections.title: The SRv6 Capabilities Sub-TLV
sections.content:
A node says that it supports the SR Segment Endpoint Node functionality of RFC 8754 by advertising an SRv6 Capabilities sub-TLV inside the Router Capability TLV of RFC 7981. The sub-TLV has Type 25 and a one-octet Length whose value is 2 plus the length of any sub-sub-TLVs. Its Flags field is two octets, and one flag is defined: the O-flag, set when the router supports use of the O-bit in the SRH as defined in RFC 9259. The remaining bits, including bit 0, are reserved for future use, must be set to zero on transmission and must be ignored on receipt. No sub-sub-TLVs are currently defined.

Algorithms are advertised separately. An SRv6-capable router indicates one or more supported algorithms by advertising the Segment Routing Algorithm sub-TLV defined in RFC 8667.
sections.plainLanguage: A router says it supports SRv6 by including a small capabilities sub-TLV in its router capability advertisement. One flag in it tells the network that the router can handle the O-bit in the segment routing header.

sections.title: Advertising Maximum SRv6 SID Depths
sections.content:
RFC 8491 defines how node-specific and link-specific values for Maximum SID Depth (MSD) are advertised: node MSDs in a sub-TLV of the Router Capability TLV, and link MSDs in a sub-TLV of TLVs 22, 23, 25, 141, 222 and 223. This document defines four SRv6 MSD types and requests assignments in the IGP MSD-Types registry.

  • Maximum Segments Left, type 41, signals the maximum value of the Segments Left field in the SRH of a received packet that the router will accept before applying the Endpoint behaviour associated with a SID. If no value is advertised, the supported value is 0.
  • Maximum End Pop, type 42, signals the maximum number of SIDs in the SRH to which the router can apply the Penultimate Segment Pop (PSP) or Ultimate Segment Pop (USP) behaviour. If the advertised value is zero, or no value is advertised, the router cannot apply PSP or USP flavours.
  • Maximum H.Encaps, type 44, signals the maximum number of SIDs that can be added to the segment list of an SRH as part of the H.Encaps behaviour. If the advertised value is zero, or no value is advertised, the headend can apply an SR Policy that contains only one segment without inserting any SRH header. A non-zero value means the headend can insert an SRH with up to the advertised number of SIDs.
  • Maximum End D, type 45, specifies the maximum number of SIDs present in an SRH when performing decapsulation. The permitted SID types include, but are not limited to, End.DX6, End.DT4, End.DT46, End with USD, and End.X with USD. If the advertised value is zero, or no value is advertised, the router cannot apply any behaviour that results in decapsulation and forwarding of the inner packet when the outer IPv6 header contains an SRH.
sections.plainLanguage: A router also has to say how deep it can go: how many segments it will accept in a header, how many it can add, and how many it can strip. These limits are advertised as Maximum SID Depth values, and each of the four types here has a number assigned to it.

sections.title: Locators, Reachability and Forwarding
sections.content:
An SRv6 Segment Identifier is 128 bits and consists of locator, function and argument parts. A node is provisioned with topology- and algorithm-specific locators for each of the topology and algorithm pairs it supports, and each locator is a covering prefix for all the SIDs provisioned on that node with the matching topology and algorithm.

Locators must be advertised in the SRv6 Locator TLV. Forwarding entries for the advertised locators must be installed in the forwarding plane of receiving SRv6-capable routers when the associated topology and algorithm are supported by the receiving node, following the process defined for the Prefix Reachability TLVs 236 and 237. Locators associated with algorithms 0 and 1 should also be advertised in a Prefix Reachability TLV, so that legacy routers install a forwarding entry for that SRv6 traffic. Where the same prefix with the same prefix length, Multi-Topology Identifier and algorithm arrives in both a Prefix Reachability TLV and an SRv6 Locator TLV, the Prefix Reachability advertisement must be preferred when installing entries, so that SRv6-capable and SRv6-incapable routers do not end up with inconsistent forwarding entries. Locators associated with Flexible Algorithms should not be advertised in the Prefix Reachability TLVs, because doing so would make the forwarding for them follow the algorithm 0 path.

SRv6 SIDs are advertised as sub-TLVs in the SRv6 Locator TLV, except for SIDs associated with a specific neighbour or link, which are advertised as sub-TLVs of TLVs 22, 23, 25, 141, 222 and 223. SIDs received from other nodes are not directly routable and must not be installed in the forwarding plane; reachability to a SID depends on the existence of a covering locator. For forwarding to work correctly, the locator must be the longest match prefix installed for those SIDs, so operators should avoid a situation where another locator associated with a different topology or algorithm is the longest match, or where another prefix advertisement is the longest match.
sections.plainLanguage: Each SRv6 segment identifier is 128 bits and starts with a locator, a prefix that covers all the segments a node owns. Receivers install a forwarding entry for the locator rather than for each individual segment, so a segment is reachable only when a covering locator has been advertised.

sections.title: The SRv6 Locator TLV and the Anycast Flag
sections.content:
The SRv6 Locator TLV is a new top-level TLV with Type 27 and a variable-length Length field. Four bits are reserved, and the rest of the first word carries the Multi-Topology Identifier, whose value 0 is legal. The TLV is followed by one or more locator entries. Each entry has a four-octet Metric, a one-octet Flags field whose D-flag carries the up and down bit of RFC 5305, a one-octet Algorithm field drawn from the IGP Algorithm Types registry of RFC 8665, and a one-octet Loc-Size field giving the number of bits in the SRv6 Locator. The Loc-Size must be from the range 1 to 128, and the entire TLV must be ignored if it is outside that range. The locator itself is 1 to 16 octets, encoded in the minimal number of octets for the given number of bits, with trailing bits set to zero and ignored on receipt. The entry ends with a one-octet sub-TLV length and the optional sub-TLVs, of which the Prefix Attribute Flags sub-TLV of RFC 7794 should be included. It must be included when the advertisement is leaked upwards in the hierarchy or originated as a result of redistribution from another protocol or another IS-IS instance, because without it receivers cannot determine the correct source of the advertisement.

Both prefixes and SRv6 Locators may be configured as anycast, so the same value can be advertised by several routers, and other routers need to know that it is an anycast identifier. A new bit in the Prefix Attribute Flags sub-TLV says so: the Anycast Flag, the A-flag, at bit 4. It should be set when the prefix or locator is configured as anycast, and must be clear otherwise. It must be preserved when the advertisement is leaked between levels. The A-flag and the N-flag must not both be set; if both are set in the advertisement, receivers must ignore the N-flag. If at least one of the routers advertising the same prefix or locator sets the A-flag, the prefix or locator should be considered anycast, and one advertised by a single node without the A-flag must be considered node specific. All the nodes advertising the same anycast locator must instantiate the exact same set of SIDs under that locator, because a failure to do so may result in traffic being dropped or misrouted.

The X-flag of the Prefix Attribute Flags sub-TLV, unlike in TLVs 236 and 237, is valid when sent in the SRv6 Locator TLV, and its state must match the embedded X-bit of any advertisement for the same prefix in TLVs 236 and 237. Where the two disagree, the flags advertised in the Prefix Reachability TLV must be preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: The new top-level TLV carries the locator entries. Each entry gives a metric, an algorithm, the size of the locator in bits and the locator itself, and it may carry flags such as the new anycast flag, which marks an address that several routers all answer for.

sections.title: The SRv6 End SID Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The SRv6 End SID sub-TLV advertises SRv6 SIDs with Endpoint behaviours that do not need a particular neighbour in order to be applied correctly. SIDs associated with a neighbour are advertised with the sub-TLVs described in the next section. The End SID sub-TLV is advertised inside the SRv6 Locator TLV, and the SIDs it carries inherit the topology and algorithm from the parent locator.

The sub-TLV has Type 5 and a variable Length. Its Flags field is one octet with no flags currently defined, all bits reserved, which must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. The Endpoint Behavior field is two octets as defined in RFC 8986, and unsupported or unrecognized behaviour values are ignored by the receiver. The SID field is 16 octets. A one-octet length field introduces optional sub-sub-TLVs, and any sub-sub-TLV not allowed in the SRv6 End SID sub-TLV must be ignored.

An SRv6 End SID must be allocated from its associated locator, and one that is not must be ignored. Multiple End SIDs may be associated with the same locator. Where the number of End SID sub-TLVs exceeds the capacity of a single TLV, multiple Locator TLVs for the same locator may be advertised, and for a given MTID and locator the algorithm must be the same in all of them; if that restriction is not met, all the TLVs for that MTID and locator must be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The End SID sub-TLV lists the segments a node has that do not depend on a particular neighbour. Each entry gives the 128-bit segment identifier and the two-octet behaviour code bound to it, and the segment must fall inside the locator that contains it.

sections.title: Advertising Adjacency SIDs and the SID Structure
sections.content:
Some Endpoint behaviours are tied to a particular adjacency. Two new sub-TLVs of TLVs 22, 23, 25, 141, 222 and 223 are defined for them: the SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV for a point-to-point adjacency, and the SRv6 LAN End.X SID sub-TLV for a LAN adjacency. IS-IS neighbour advertisements are topology specific but not algorithm specific, so SIDs advertised in these two sub-TLVs inherit the topology from the associated neighbour advertisement, while the algorithm is specified in the individual SID. Every SID advertised in them must be a subnet of a locator with matching topology and algorithm that the same node advertises in an SRv6 Locator TLV; SIDs that do not meet this requirement must be ignored.

The SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV has Type 43. Its one-octet Flags field carries a B-flag marking the SID as eligible for protection, for example with IP Fast Reroute; an S-flag meaning the SID refers to a set of adjacencies and may therefore be assigned to other adjacencies as well; and a P-flag meaning the SID is persistently allocated, so its value stays the same across a router restart or an interface flap. The remaining bits are reserved. The sub-TLV also carries the Algorithm, a Weight used for load balancing, the two-octet Endpoint Behavior, the 16-octet SID and optional sub-sub-TLVs. The SRv6 LAN End.X SID sub-TLV has Type 44 and the same B-, S- and P-flags, Algorithm, Weight, Endpoint Behavior and SID fields. Because the parent TLV advertises the adjacency to the Designated Intermediate System for the LAN, the LAN sub-TLV also carries the System-ID of the physical neighbour on the LAN that the SID is associated with, and several of these sub-TLVs may be associated with the same LAN.

All three SID sub-TLVs may carry an optional SRv6 SID Structure sub-sub-TLV, of Type 1, which advertises the length in bits of the four parts of a SID: Locator Block, Locator Node, Function and Argument. It must not appear more than once in its parent sub-TLV, and the sum of the four sizes must be no more than 128 bits, or the parent sub-TLV is ignored. This information is intended for the control and management planes and must not be used at a transit node for forwarding packets. The RFC gives two example uses: validating the SRv6 SIDs instantiated in the network, which a controller can learn through BGP-LS and then monitor for conformance to the allocation scheme chosen by the operator; and verification and automation for securing an SRv6 domain by provisioning filtering rules at the boundaries of that domain.

Which behaviours may be advertised where is fixed. A behaviour must only be advertised in the TLVs marked Y in the table, and must not be advertised in those marked N. End, including its PSP, USP and USD flavours, is advertised in the End SID sub-TLV. End.X, including its PSP, USP and USD flavours, and End.DX6 and End.DX4, are advertised in the End.X and LAN End.X sub-TLVs. End.DT6, End.DT4 and End.DT46 are advertised in the End SID sub-TLV. Not every behaviour defined in RFC 8986 is covered here; End.T is not.
sections.plainLanguage: Segments that belong to a particular link are advertised next to that neighbour, in two new sub-TLVs, one for point-to-point links and one for LANs. A further sub-TLV records how the 128 bits of a segment are split into a locator, a function and an argument, which helps operators check that their own numbering scheme is being followed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security concerns for IS-IS are addressed in ISO 10589, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310. While IS-IS is deployed under a single administrative domain, there can be deployments where potential attackers have access to one or more networks in the IS-IS routing domain, and in those deployments the stronger authentication mechanisms defined in those documents should be used.

The security considerations for Segment Routing are discussed in RFC 8402. RFC 8986 defines the SRv6 Network Programming concept and the main SR behaviours that enable interoperable overlays, and its security considerations apply here too. The RFC also notes that an advertisement for an incorrect MSD value may have negative consequences, with further considerations in RFC 8491, and points to the security concerns of the O-flag in RFC 9259 and of Flexible Algorithms in RFC 9350.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds no protection of its own. It points at the existing IS-IS authentication documents, and at the security discussions for Segment Routing and for SRv6 network programming.

viz.caption: The four SRv6 Maximum SID Depth types

items.title: 41, SRH Max SL
items.text: The largest Segments Left value the router accepts in a received packet before it applies the endpoint behaviour of a SID. If nothing is advertised, the supported value is 0.

items.title: 42, SRH Max End Pop
items.text: The largest number of SIDs in the header to which the router can apply the Penultimate Segment Pop or Ultimate Segment Pop behaviour. Zero or nothing advertised means it cannot.

items.title: 44, SRH Max H.encaps
items.text: The largest number of SIDs the headend can add to the segment list as part of the H.Encaps behaviour. Zero or nothing advertised means it can only use a policy with one segment and no SRH header.

items.title: 45, SRH Max End D
items.text: The largest number of SIDs present in the header when the router decapsulates. Zero or nothing advertised means it cannot apply a behaviour that decapsulates and forwards the inner packet.
